articles.title: The Goal of Contemporary Journalism
articles.text:
The Goal of Contemporary Journalism
Jeffrey Goldberg, Amna Nawaz, and Joe Kahn discussed how to sustain a free press in an era of public distrust, social-media punditry, and a hostile federal government.
In a conversation at The Atlantic Festival, Jeffrey Goldberg, The Atlantic’s editor in chief, spoke with Amna Nawaz, a co-anchor and co-managing editor of PBS NewsHour, and Joe Kahn, the executive editor of The New York Times, about the state of independent media.
In his second term, Donald Trump has escalated his confrontations with the press. The New York Times was personally sued by Trump for $15 billion and, separately, the paper’s journalists were recently served subpoenas for reporting on the Qatari jet gifted to the White House. (The Department of Justice subsequently withdrew these subpoenas.) Federal support for PBS was scrapped last year. And as self-styled journalists proliferate online, public trust in the media is at record lows. Evan Smith, the panel’s moderator and The Atlantic’s managing director for events, referred to the guests as outliers for having weathered these attacks—“You’ve survived.” Nawaz responded, “I wouldn’t put it in the past tense. We are surviving.”
With so many “content creators” and pundits now claiming to be journalists, Goldberg reflected on how the internet has changed the journalism industry. “There was this view for a while—in the last 20 years—that the democratization of media was an unadulterated good thing,” he noted. Indeed, for decades, the media was “too stringent about who gets to talk.” But with that shift, “standards were lowered. Standards for what counts as actual verified information.”
Public distrust in the media, and the president’s frequent attacks on reporters and their employers, have made the work of journalism more difficult. “I remember, back in 2017, boarding a plane with my then-4-year-old daughter, and the man ahead of us was wearing a T-shirt that said in block letters on the back: Journalist. Tree. Rope. Some assembly required,” Nawaz said. To restore public faith, the panelists agreed that journalists need to be transparent about the work that they do. “The further that news and information travels away from the individual human-being journalists who do the work, the less trust there is,” Kahn said. “Original reporting is still by far the most valuable thing.” He later added: “Kind of objectively, I think we’re killing it.”
The following conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Evan Smith: What is the job of journalism today? Jeff, we talked about this when you were on my PBS show a few months ago. Here’s what you said: “The goal of any quality journalism operation these days is to put as much truth into the universe as possible.” Say more about that, please.
Jeffrey Goldberg: I continue to agree with what I said to you on your show. I endorse my statement of six months ago. There’s two levels of your question, “What do editors in chief do?,” and mostly what we do is keep things moving. Tinker. Try to go deep on the problems that exist day to day. The last 11 years have helped us focus on core tasks. We thought most questions were settled: The First Amendment is the First Amendment; the freedom of the press is vitally important; the media plays an indispensable role in any democracy.
These things have come under pressure. That’s bad for civilization, that they’re under pressure and that these questions are unsettled. It’s good for us in the sense that it helps clarify the purpose. So you wake up every morning with even more of a sense of mission than maybe you would in ordinary times. I am not saying that we are politicized. I always tell our staff this, and I’m borrowing from Marty Baron, the former editor of The Washington Post: We’re not going to war. We’re not part of the resistance. We’re just going to work. And as long as you just remember that your job every day is to find out something that’s true, contextualize it, treat it fairly, and write it accurately, that’s great. You finished the day by putting something out there. You hope that people are taking to it. You hope that it elevates the ideology of truth. But that’s what you do. It’s sad that these concepts are under pressure. I can only speak for myself, but it’s great to wake up with that purpose.
Smith: Joe, I would agree with Jeff. This is an extraordinary moment. Truth isn’t truth. Feelings are facts. Reality is subjective. Conspiracy theories and misinformation are running rampant. It is harder than ever to meet the Goldberg standard, isn’t it?
Joe Kahn: It is. And the task for us is to do, as Jeffrey said, to wake up every day, to do original reporting. Ideally, bring new information to light on all the stories that matter every day, and to get it out there, increasingly in forms that people want to consume that information. And that mission is under stress, but it’s more critical than ever. And it makes the job even more vital to American democracy than it ever was. And I would really emphasize the original reporting and new information. We’re in an environment where people feel like they can get information in their feeds nonstop, 24 hours a day. It’s buzzing at them on their phones. They’re hearing it in their AirPods, but actual new original reporting that relies on expert reporters who are going to the scene of news, who are asking tough questions, is in short supply, and it’s on us to find a way to get that to more people.
Smith: Amna, the stakes could not be higher in this extraordinary moment. Or, at least, that’s what we all keep saying over and over. Informed communities strengthen democracy. Uninformed communities weaken democracy. It’s a little grandiose-sounding. But speaking of truth, that is true. Those are the stakes.
Amna Nawaz: Information is power. That is a basic fact. And in a democracy, an informed electorate is what powers our democracy. That’s also a basic fact. I couldn’t agree more with everything that Joe and Jeff just said. I look at it as the advice I got from my very first boss in journalism. He told me that to be a good journalist is a lot like just being a good person in life: Most of it is showing up. You have to show up. And that means showing up on the ground. It means going to cover the stories that not everybody is covering. It means reporting from the front lines. It also means showing up when you’re able to have access to someone in a position of power to hold them accountable. The way I think about my job every single day is: I’m not asking questions that I necessarily want the answers to. I’m asking questions on behalf of everyone out there who can’t be in that room, who can’t put questions to that person in power. The threats that we’re up against now, they’re not like anything we faced in recent times. I compare it to some of the stuff that I’ve seen covering other countries, other autocratic, anti-democratic leaders in other nations. The same hallmarks are happening here now. It’s a worrying time for journalists, but the best we can do every day is show up and, as I like to say, just put something good out into the world every day.
Smith: Jeff, the job of journalism, isn’t it also to set an agenda of sorts to tee up the things for people that they should stop and pay attention to in their busy lives? The curatorial piece of this, the choices we make, that is also part of our job.
Goldberg: There was this view for a while, in the last 20 years, that the democratization of media was an unadulterated good thing. Obviously, the First Amendment allows anyone with a piece of paper and a pencil to become a journalist. That’s great. And what happened was the barriers to entry lowered, obviously because of the internet, and everybody thought that was a good thing. But standards were lowered. Standards for what counts as actual verified information. It actually—believe it or not—takes training and practice and more practice and more practice to get it right as a reporter. You can’t just jump into this on the deep end. We were having a very polite dinner party in the media probably until 20, 25 years ago. And then, somebody described to me, the barbarians put ladders up and came up and started squatting on the dining-room table. And this person, obviously an older journalist, thought this was a straight-up bad idea. We probably, as an institution, were too stringent about who gets to talk and who doesn’t get to talk, or who doesn’t have their voices amplified.
But now, it is a chaos of misinformation and bad motivation. I’m not saying we’re perfect. God knows. Right? But we’ve got to go back to finding a balance, and we have to explain to people how we do what we do and why we do what we do. Show the work. We have succeeded on any day in which we find out something new that is true and tell that truth, despite the fact that other powerful people don’t want us to tell it. I would just add something to what Joe said. We had Maggie Haberman here yesterday, and John Swan. And Maggie gets a certain amount of criticism, as any famous reporter gets, but something Joe said just kind of triggered this in me. It’s like, half of the things we know about what the Trump administration does is because Maggie has told us. Seriously. I’ll line up a million bloggers and Twitch streamers or whatever and put them against one Maggie. And I know that Maggie’s delivered more right than they’ve ever delivered. They deliver attitude. But Maggie’s got facts.
Kahn: Original reporting is still by far the most valuable thing. And it still breaks through——real knowledge and sources and doggedness on the beat and the ability to kind of cut through the spin. People ask, WWhat’s going on with trust in the media? What even is “the media”?? The media is now thousands of influencers online. It’s opinion journalists. It’s self-appointed arbiters of information of all kinds. A tiny, tiny fraction of them actually do original reporting. And that’s what matters more than anything else. And it does break through. Because it’s verified information. It’s factual. It matters. It’s important. And people like Maggie have a track record of getting it right, cycle after cycle, story after story. It matters more than ever. And it does break through.
Nawaz: Can I just add to that too? I think when we talk about the way the content moves these days, the fact that our original journalism is out there competing in the same messy and noisy landscape as millions of other content creators, you know, doing TikTok dances in their kitchens. But at the same time, I have this conversation with some very powerful podcasters recently who are not and would not identify themselves as journalists. They rely on our work. They use our original journalism to fuel their conversations and to have something that they can rely on to talk about to their hundreds of millions of followers. And so I think that’s not necessarily a bad thing. There’s an amplification to the work because it gets out in various forms.
Smith: But they’re not the same thing.
Nawaz: They are not the same thing. And I think most of them would say that they are not journalists.
Smith: Joe, let me ask you, in the context of The New York Times specifically——because The New York Times is one of one,, as opposed to one of many,, as a news source for so many people around this country and around the world—d—do you think, as it relates to setting an agenda, you are meeting the moment? Are you making the right choices, and are you framing your journalism out to the world in a way that the agenda is being set the way it should be said?
Goldberg: Just say yes.
Kahn: Kind of objectively, I think we’re killing it.
Smith: That may be the only quote from this panel.
Kahn: The big battle, in my view, is both to keep the best reporters on the most sensitive subjects at a time when they’re absolutely, relentlessly under attack. Motivated and protected by the full force of our security personnel—physical and cybersecurity—and legal support when they’re almost inevitably going to come under legal pressure for doing the kind of reporting that matters. And then also simultaneously finding a way to get it out there in people’s feeds in a way that they want to consume it, and not waiting and relying for them to come to us. And we’re doing both of those things at scale at the moment. We have a long way to go, but I’m really proud of the work that we’ve been able to do in this environment. And by the way, I think we’re winning, honestly. We’re under a lot of pressure,, and I mean, all of us,, wwe’re past the point where people were worried about whether good--quality free press can stand up in this moment in America and still show its resolve, provide good original reporting, withstand the pressure. We’re doing it. And that particular pillar of democracy is strong.
Smith: Well, certainly at the national level. We’ll come to local in a little bit. I’m not sure that it’s exactly the same in the middle of the country. I want to ask, though, Jeff, about the people on the receiving end of this. Our readers and our viewers in communities around the country, are they paying attention? Is this a conversation, back to the dinner--party idea, that only we’re having? Or are they actually in the conversation as well about the importance of a free press and the state of journalism? Do they share the view that a free press is important? Do they get that the work we do matters? Do they even understand what that work is? That’s a question I’ve got.
Goldberg: It’s an interesting question because,, again, I would just echo what Joe said, the media is a useless term for the type of media we’re talking about. Sometimes, we tend to believe that we do our work and the work is self-explanatory. And everybody has the same civic understanding of the importance of the press. The kind of Jeffersonian understanding: Better to have a free press than a government, even. It’s not true. Can I tell you a very quick story?
Smith: Sure, please.
Goldberg: It’s The Atlantic Festival. I can do it. I’m allowed. I paid for this microphone!
(Laughter.)
Smith: The name’s on the building.
Goldberg: This is a really revelatory moment for me, and it changed my understanding of what we have to do to explain the importance of our work and how we do our work. So, in 2020, six years ago, I wrote a story about Donald Trump’s attitude toward veterans and the military. The shorthand of it became “suckers” and “losers.” That he had called WWI veterans buried in a cemetery that he didn’t want to visit because it was raining: He said they’re “suckers” and “losers.” The story was based on my reporting from four anonymous sources. I cited four anonymous sources in the story. Subsequently, by the way, John Kelly, the former White House chief of staff, Marine general, came out and publicly validated it. So, I can say that, but at the time, it was an anonymously sourced story. The White House did what the White House does, right? This was right before the election in 2020. A lot of pressure, a lot of heat, a lot of attacks. I was speaking a couple of months after the story came out, to a group, and someone gets up, an intelligent person, and says something I don’t understand: “Why would you publish a story based on information given to you by people you don’t even know?” And I didn’t understand the question, and I said, “What do you mean?” He says, “Well, you said you had four anonymous sources, but you don’t even know who they are.”
 
 (Laughter.)
My instinct was to laugh, too, but like, it’s not his fault. And I said “No, no, they’re not anonymous to me. I know them. I know them.” Then I explained the methodology of the information gathering and how we use fact-checking and verified it. And at first I was like, “Oh, wow, that guy doesn’t know much.” And then I thought, “Wait, if people don’t understand what I’m doing, that’s on me as much as it is on them.” And by the way, we’re going to feel this more and more. This is already happening in Europe, where nefarious forces are arguing that what we would think of as probing sources—knocking on doors, calling people up repeatedly, trying to get them to talk to us—this is becoming redefined as harassment, not reporting in a democracy. So we’re going to have to do a much better job of explaining sources and methods and the importance of it. I go back to this Maggie point. You’re criticizing The New York Times for X, Y, and Z. But the only reason you know about X, Y, and Z is because of The New York Times.
Smith: Amna, you mentioned threats. I want to talk to the three of you about the threats in the world right now. They come from people in power and they take many forms. They’re financial. They’re legal. They’re political. And, amazingly, they’re physical. It’s not lost on me that the three institutions represented on this stage are exhibits A, B, and C of the new normal. The Atlantic is the subject at the moment of a defamation suit by the FBI director. We stand by our reporting. We’re vigorously defending against that suit. Earlier this year, subpoenas were delivered to the homes of New York Times reporters after reporting on the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One. Subsequently, the Department of Justice “voluntarily” withdrew those subpoenas. Voluntarily in big, fluffy air quotes. PBS has been defunded, and yet you’re still standing here.
Nawaz: Yes, we are.
Smith: But I also need to say that you’re the outliers, in the sense that you’ve survived what I’ve just described. A lot of news organizations don’t have the resources or the stomach to stand up for themselves. They’re either folding in advance, anticipatory obedience, or after the fact. We live in capitulation nation as it relates to these threats. A lot of knee-bending going on, a lot of settlements being paid, a lot of favor being curried. Joe, when you look out at our industry, do you think we’re showing our best selves in response to some of these threats?
Nawaz: Can I just say, I’m speaking only on behalf of PBS: Yeah, I think we are. And here’s why. One of the reasons is, as you mentioned, we’ve been defunded. The president made it very clear from the get that he wanted to defund all public media. And we, as part of our mission, remain free for anyone to access all of our content any of the time. So nothing goes behind a paywall. You don’t subscribe to see our journalism. I’m not sure I share Joe’s optimism that we are winning, I will say, and you use the word you’ve survived, I wouldn’t put it in the past tense. We are surviving. But I think we are very much in it. And I don’t think we know how this ends up until we get through it, whatever that looks like. The only way out, to underscore the point you made, is through. And that’s what we have to do every day. It is the journalism that we do every day. It’s the 330 local member stations fighting for their own survival out there on the PBS network. But I am not as optimistic because I’ve seen what’s happened in other countries. We talk about threats and we say it kind of vaguely as if it’s become normal because it has. It is a feature, it is not a bug, of the current political climate.
And you go all the way back to a president who ran and called journalists “scum” and “enemies of the people.” I remember back in 2017, boarding a plane with my then-4-year-old daughter and the man ahead of us wearing a T-shirt that said in block letters on the back: Journalist. Tree. Rope. Some assembly required. And me praying that my 4-year-old would not start to sound out the words, as she was doing at the time. That is not normal and it has become normal, and we’re seeing it show up in polling with people increasingly saying things like, Yeah, maybe the government should be able to say when journalists can’t report on something or should have to take a story down because it risks national security. We are in a new normal for this nation.
Smith: Yeah. I mean, Joe, I’m going to take Amna’s words here seriously. It does not do justice to the severity or the significance of these threats to say they’re mere shots across the bow. This is a sea change.
Kahn: I agree with that. I think just the price of defending against these lawsuits that Trump is throwing around with his very large and essentially full-time legal staff, suing everybody who writes an article that puts him on the defensive in some way. We have a $15 billion lawsuit from Trump. It’s a full-time activity for some of our legal staff, for outside legal counsel. These things cost millions of dollars to defend. The New York Times is in a pretty strong position, so we can defend them. But if you’re another type of organization and you don’t have those resources, then the threat of a lawsuit or the existence of a lawsuit is itself a deterrent.
Smith: It changes behavior.
Kahn: It does change it, and it does have an effect. So I acknowledge that. When I’m saying that I think we’re winning, I think if you still step back and look at the overall information environment in this country, it still is vigorous. It still wants to be free. There is a huge amount of debate unfolding in the public space. There’s still really good original reporting being done by quality journalists, both locally and nationally every day, and it is not going to be suppressed. That’s what I mean when we’re winning: It won’t be suppressed. That doesn’t mean that the cost of defending it doesn’t go up. But I’m really confident in the essential, kind of, American essence that this is a country that wants free speech, that’s going to protect free speech. And Donald Trump or any other president isn’t going to shut that down.
Smith: Amna, I want to come back to you because I’m personally obsessed with one aspect of these threats, in particular. Women journalists are a special target in this moment. I’m going to say their names. Rachel Scott of ABC the other day, Kristen Holmes of CNN, Catherine Lucey from Bloomberg, to whom the president said “Quiet, piggy.” Kristen Welker threatened the other day with sanctions by the FCC for merely saying on the air that the president’s endorsements had not gone super well. Maggie Haberman, always. All for doing their jobs. We seem to have almost legitimized or normalized that in our response, seems like. I can’t understand why there’s not more outrage in the press corps every time one of these women who asks a question of the president is treated the way she’s treated, why everybody en masse doesn’t walk out.
Nawaz: I take your point. I think I share your outrage and your concern. I will say, hats off to the women who are in that position every day, because I know the only thing they’re thinking about in that moment is the next question. That’s the only thing that they’re thinking about, because they’re pros and that’s what they show up to do. So I don’t even know that they want everybody to walk out. They would rather stay and continue to put tough questions to the president to be able to get answers on behalf of the people they serve. Again, it is a feature, not a bug. And that kind of misogyny, that kind of focus on women, we’ve seen much more aggressive stances against reporters of color, female reporters of color in particular, over the last 10-odd years. That is also a hallmark of autocratic and anti-democratic leaders around the world. There have been books and studies published on this, and it is becoming normalized, as you say. I mean, we can shout it out. We can point it out every time it happens. But because it happens so frequently and because there is so much else to cover, and there’s so many other headlines that those reporters themselves under attack want to focus on, we move on.
Smith: I’m glad you brought up Marty Baron’s famous line from the first administration. Something to the effect of, as you said, Our job is not to go to war. Our job is to go to work. That’s the response to these threats from your perspective, whether it’s the chair of the FCC or the president’s social-media feed. We fight back with journalism, right?
Goldberg: But going back to this point you’re making about who’s doing well and who’s not. The foundation of everything here is ownership that is stalwart. Marty Baron then was working for a Jeff Bezos who believed in the mission. That was then. Now is now. I mean, strangely, I’m the recipient of his moral incognizance, in the sense that we’ve hired close to 40 Washington Post journalists in the last year because they want to do journalism. But it all has to do with Sulzberger’s understanding the purpose of their institution and willing to stand up for the institution. And if you don’t mind me saying, it has to do with the owner of The Atlantic, who is stalwart about these things. And you’ve made the point. There’s a lot of different institutions on the TV side, on the print side, that simply don’t have strong, ethical, brave leaders. And I would say—I don’t even know if she’s here, but I’m saying it anyway. And I’m not blowing smoke at all; I really feel this—that we could not do anything if we didn’t know that the ownership had our back. I would only say, the perfect example of this is when I got involved in that Signal mess last year.
Nawaz: Wait, what happened? Something happened?
(Laughter.)
Smith: Everybody, cancel your 10 o’clock.
Goldberg: When I got involved in that situation, it was very, very fraught. I mean, our lawyers had lawyers, and those lawyers had lawyers. Right now our general counsel is having a sharp intake of breath because he never knows what I’m going to say about this. But the very brief version of that—and I think Joe has probably experienced this and Amna has experienced this with PBS management—eventually the information reaches the ownership level. And Here’s the situation, and This is what we want to do. And the word from on high was, If it’s true and it’s important, publish it. And that sounds like basic journalism ownership. But not these days. And so that is the crucial difference. I’m very, very happy to have all these colleagues from my former newspaper The Washington Post join The Atlantic. I’m not happy about what happened at The Washington Post. We need strong newspapers in America, and you only have strong newspapers if you have strong leadership and ownership.
Kahn: Right. Can I add one thing to that?
Smith: You may, of course.
Kahn: The Atlantic I know is celebrating its 169th year. The New York Times yesterday celebrated its 175th. So we’re ahead of you by a little bit.
Goldberg: But we’re gonna catch up. We’re right on your tail.
(Laughter.)
Kahn: We both have, in our mission statement, the word independence. Independent for 169 years, independent for 175 years. It’s another word that we use a lot, independent. And I’m not sure that everybody always appreciates what independence actually means. We know what it means to be independent of political partisan views. And we profess ourselves as journalists not to be partisans. And that’s true. But it also means independence of ownership, honestly. And the independence of ownership is increasingly important in this moment. And PBS experienced that because you receive money from the government and now you don’t. And that’s a pressure point. If you’re owned by a giant corporation that has a lot of other interests that are also regulated by the government, and they can manipulate or pull those levers, that is also not true independence. True independence is financial stability and independent ownership that does not have too many other interests that are at the discretion of the government to interfere with. And protecting independent journalism really does mean protecting those independent owners and supporting those independent owners.
Nawaz: To that point, can I just say—to underscore your point about the fact that we as journalists can’t do our jobs without backers who want us to do the journalism, and underscoring your point that people want good journalism—the way that PBS viewers, viewers like you, stepped up.
Goldberg: We’re one minute from handing out tote bags, by the way.
Nawaz: I’m available outside, if you need help navigating to the website. But it does underscore both those points because people wanted to see good journalism. When our funding got cut, people did step up there. That is heartening.
Goldberg: By the way, just to add, I’m sure most of you are New York Times subscribers, the day the Sulzbergers buy rocket ships is the day you should start worrying, right?
Smith: Right.
Goldberg: That’s a bad sign.
Smith: Joe, you mentioned trust earlier, and you talked about how hard it is in an environment in which “the media” is not what we always thought of as “the media.” But I want to push on this a little bit because I do look at the Gallup surveys every year of the American public’s trust in media. Two years ago, the annual survey showed that 31 percent of the public had a “great deal” of trust or a “fair amount” of trust in the media. This was a historic low. This was in 2024. And I thought, Well, we’re in the basement. No place to go but up. They do the survey in 2025; turns out there’s another basement. Now we’re down to 28 percent. This is the new historic low in trust in the media. By the way, in case you’re wondering, the high was 72 percent, in 1976, 50 years ago. “No trust at all” in this last survey was 34 percent, a third of the country. And for those of us who live in red states, I do, that are run by Republican leaders—in case you’re wondering, they did it by party—Republicans as a party, 8 percent have a “great deal” of trust in the media. How did we get here? It’s not just the confusion between traditional journalism and people on TikTok. How did we get here?
Kahn: We live in a deeply polarized and partisan moment with a very confusing landscape that is called media. But there are some elements that are real and they’re challenges for us. You mentioned the Gallup survey. There’s also been a lot of Reuters work on this, and we’ve looked at those numbers really closely. And it’s very interesting that the further that news and information travels away from the individual human-being journalists who do the work, the less trust there is. So that most trust is still to the credible, hardworking, independent, real reporters on the beat, doing the job, knocking on doors, getting information and relaying that information, ideally in conversational terms, directly to the people who are consuming it. The more you move away from it toward platforms, toward social media, and at the low end of the spectrum, filtered through artificial intelligence, the less trust there is in the quality of that information. That’s all called media. But for us, what we’re trying to do to address this is to make more transparent the work that individual journalists are doing on the ground, putting their own expertise out there, making themselves vulnerable to get the information and then conveying that to the users of that as best as possible. Because it’s human beings; it’s a value that human beings bring to help explain and unearth new information that I think can help us.
Smith: So that’s how we got here, and that’s also where we go from here.
Kahn: I think.
Goldberg: Don’t forget, there are active campaigns being run against the idea of independent journalism.
Smith: 100 percent percent.
Goldberg: This is what I meant before. Just because we’re not interested in that war doesn’t mean that war isn’t happening. And so people like Steve Bannon, and people on the left too, for that matter, it’s in their interest to undermine through lying the nature of what we do. And we again sit here and say the work speaks for itself, but the work doesn’t. But we also have to speak up. We have to almost lobby for ourselves and say, Look, there are people whose interest it is to undermine the idea that there’s some kind of fair truth out there.
Smith: Let’s accept that there has been an intentional effort, call it the last 10 years, to undermine faith and confidence in a lot of institutions that hold people in power accountable. The media is just one. The plan is working as intended. But isn’t it also true that we own some of this as an industry? The call’s coming from inside the house? We’ve done some of this to ourselves.
Nawaz: I think, to some of the points that have been made earlier, I think we’ve taken for granted the idea that people would just trust the information that we put out there because they always had. There was an idea that these are credible legacy institutions.
Smith: Right.
Nawaz: To your point, back in 1976, the trust was high and we thought that would just continue. The 1976 media landscape was a universe away from where we are today. I mean, I wasn’t even born. Sorry, Jeff.
(Laughter.)
Goldberg: I actually didn’t hear what she said. I don’t know what she’s apologizing for. I’ll just accept your apology.
Smith: Turn on your hearing aid.
Nawaz: I will say, when you ask people about the media, I think there’s sort of a generalized—yes, there’s merchants of misinformation, people who attack the media as mistrustful and are agenda-driven. And so they automatically say, Yes, we don’t trust the media the same way we don’t trust Congress or we don’t trust the Supreme Court. All institutions are under that same skepticism. When you ask people individually, do you trust The New York Times? Do you trust The Atlantic?
Smith: Well, PBS always indexes at the top of that list.
Nawaz: We are second among most trusted brands right now, second only to the Weather Channel. Shoutout to the Weather Channel. And I think the same thing is true at the local level. To Joe’s point, people trust the people in their own community. They trust their local journalist, people they know, and we have to work harder on building those connections.
Smith: So we have a minute left. Let’s solve the local journalism problem in one minute.
Goldberg: But by the way, the solution to the national problem is at the local level. Which is to say that if there’s one problem that I would identify as our own fault, it’s hiring journalists who are trained at the same 50 colleges, and they have the same set of assumptions about the world. And, you know, The Harvard Crimson is great, but not everybody should come from the Harvard Crimson to our newsrooms. And there are a certain set of liberal assumptions that come in more than conservative assumptions. And to solve the problem, you recruit journalists and train journalists in places where people think slightly differently. It doesn’t mean that you can bring in people who can be fair and balanced, to borrow a slogan, into your newsrooms who just come from different backgrounds and have a different set of baseline assumptions. We’d be better off.
Kahn: From The Daily Pennsylvanian.
Goldberg: Yeah, no, no, the working-class Daily Pennsylvanian. And you solve that problem—we’re really on the back foot on that—by having robust journalism presences in red states, in communities where we don’t draw journalists from: veterans, evangelical Christians, so on. And we have to do a better job of diversifying in all kinds of ways, the people who come in. Because they bring in their own experiences and they question implicit assumptions that people make. I’m not saying that there’s a liberal bias in the stories you read day to day. I think that there are—if you’re not careful about it, and I know that Joe tries to be careful about it, I try to be careful about it—just unspoken assumptions that people make about the way the world is organized. And that’s not great. That’s not the main problem. The main problem is that there’s a war against us, and that war is against the idea of truth. But these are things that we have to think about.
Smith: So we end where we began. I would love to have more time to talk to you all, but we have a full day ahead of us. Please give a big hand to Amna Nawaz, Joe Kahn, and Jeffrey Goldberg.

articles.title: Báo Tiền Phong phát động chương trình ‘Chai nhựa tái sinh, hành trình tiếp nối’ 2026
articles.text: TPO - Sáng 17/9, tại Trường Đại học Phenikaa (Hà Nội), Báo Tiền Phong phối hợp cùng Coca-Cola Việt Nam phát động chương trình “Chai nhựa tái sinh, hành trình tiếp nối” năm 2026. Bước sang năm thứ tư, chương trình tiếp tục mở rộng quy mô, thúc đẩy thói quen phân loại rác tại nguồn và lan tỏa lối sống xanh trong giới trẻ.

articles.title: Lina Khan on Doomer Panic and Ending AI Exceptionalism
articles.text:
Lina Khan on Doomer Panic and Ending AI Exceptionalism
Why the AI-alarmism conversation feels off
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
As “rogue” AI agents hack systems and leaders warn of catastrophe, who should be held responsible? Former FTC Commissioner Lina Khan argues that the United States already has a lot of the regulatory tools needed. In this live episode from The Atlantic Festival, the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Khan about why the AI-alarmism conversation feels a little off, how money affects politics and regulation, and some of the ways she would be dealing with AI if she were still the head of the FTC.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel. And this is Galaxy Brain, a show where today we’re gonna talk about what on earth to do about the AI companies who are saying their products might kill us all. And I’ve got quite literally the perfect person to talk about this with, the chair of New York City’s Economic Development Corporation and the former chair of the FTC under Joe Biden, Lina Khan. But first, a little bit of background.
A bit more than a week ago, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, quit his job and he published a warning: The AI companies, he argued, were not taking safety seriously and they were, quote, “gambling with our lives.” The product that he’d spent the past three years working on was spiraling out of the control of the people who were building it, and it might someday, he said, end humanity. His warning echoed what AI executives, researchers, effective altruists on forums, and Bay Area doomers have been anxiously posting about and writing best-selling books about for more than a decade.
But Coxon’s warning did what all those other warnings failed to do. It broke containment, and it created a national conversation. Concerned lawmakers called for emergency AI meetings; President Obama weighed in; Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk all came to a rare consensus and called for a slowdown of AI development. President Donald Trump responded to all of it by calling AI fears “a hoax.” Things are moving fast. But one thing is clear: The AI-safety conversation is happening at a global scale among insiders and normies alike.
And there are almost unending questions here: How real is this threat? Is this hype and AI-company marketing? But no matter where you land on the actual risk of these companies, there is a question about what we should do about it. The companies themselves are calling for a regulatory framework, including independent auditors of the models. But not everyone’s convinced. Is all of this progress, or are the tech companies simply trying to get favorable, cushy terms that lock them into virtual monopolies? In other words, is all of their talk earnest, or is this a power grab?
What should AI-company regulation look like? Why is nobody holding these companies accountable right now? Do we need new laws? Or should we be using the existing ones better? What are the historical parallels here? Are we in uncharted waters, or is this a normal crisis that is playing out at abnormal speed and abnormal scale?
Lina Khan has spent her career wrestling with a lot of these questions, specifically as they apply to Silicon Valley’s tech giants. As FTC chair, she was part of a genuine shift in antitrust enforcement, arguing that traditional U.S. competition laws were broken and ill-suited for digital platforms.
Now, late last week, as the AI debate was roiling, Khan posted on X that the AI regulation needed to take into account that “law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products.”
So what does enforcement look like in this AI moment? Where do we go from here? I spoke with Lina Khan on Thursday morning in New York at The Atlantic Festival. Here’s our conversation.
[Music]
Warzel: Thank you all for coming. I appreciate it. Thank you, Lina, for coming here.
Lina Khan: Great to be here.
Warzel: I want to just dive in. We have limited time here. And I wanted to start with the news that has been all-consuming in the tech and political spheres over the last week or so, which is the AI-research whistleblowers warning of AI agents spinning out of control that might “kill us all.” Calls from Sam Altman, Dario [Amodei], Elon Musk, others to slow down development, quote “pace the frontier.” You weighed in on the regulatory angle on X recently. But first I just wanted to ask, why do you think this safety panic is breaking through now?
Khan: Well, I think we’ve been seeing it for the last few years, you know, various predictions about what may happen with these tools. And it certainly seems like there have been various inflection points where people within these companies have seen what they would describe potentially as a step change in terms of certain capabilities. It seems like most recently, there have been more instances of agents basically becoming more overtly defective. Some people may call them rogue, really exceeding the parameters of what people and humans had set up them to do. And so that seems to be the latest catalyst.
But I think there’s been, you know, a drumbeat in the background now for several years, including when I was back at the FTC, when we were already starting to confront less these existential questions around, you know, Could we see the eradication of humanity? and more of the bread and butter of How are these tools already impacting people in their day-to-day? I mean, for most Americans, the way they interact with AI is through a chatbot and trying to get customer service, and instead being stuck in some doom loop. Right? So I think there are a lot of ways that this is manifesting, and I think the regulatory-policy conversation can happen across that spectrum.
Warzel: Some of the concern, I think, too, comes from this idea that the models that these companies have trained and, you know, that power a lot of these chatbots, they are themselves very—they’re part of this black box. Right? Like, we don’t really know exactly what’s going into them with the weights, with the training, all of that. When you were at the FTC, when this was all kind of very young and new, what kind of sense did you get about that level of transparency and what we can’t see?
Khan: I mean, there’s a tremendous amount that we can’t see, which is not unique in terms of, you know, the relationship between an enforcer or regulator and a company, but certainly seems to be even more acute in this context. But, you know, we were already encountering black-box algorithms. And what does an enforcer do when it’s really an algorithm that is, you know, resulting in various types of products being shown or not being shown? And what does that mean for our existing laws?
I do think one pattern that we’ve seen across various moments when a new technology hits is that there can be this rush to create some exceptionalism around it, especially vis-à-vis the existing laws and regulations. And so one thing that was very important to me when I was serving in government was to make very clear that there was not any AI exemption from existing laws on the books. And I think we see, even now, a strain in the conversation around new regulation that seems to assume that these current developments are happening in some legal vacuum. And that is just false.
Like, you know, if you’re working on one of these companies, you still have an existing obligation to abide by, you know, consumer-protection laws, antidiscrimination laws, antitrust laws, product-liability regimes. And so part of what I’ve tried to, you know, include in the conversation is this realization that we may want to talk about new rules and regulations. And I think there’s a good case for it. But let’s not forget that existing legal obligations absolutely apply. And some of what we’re hearing from these firms and their executives suggests that the legal care that is already required of these firms is not being taken.
Warzel: Why do you think that everyone in the industry is behaving—and even, you know, some politicians are behaving—like these companies are exempt? What is the reason for that?
Khan: It’s a great question. I mean, I think part of it absolutely stems back to how the firms themselves market their capabilities. And when there is a push for regulation—I mean, we’ve seen this even in, you know, context around crypto, where there was a push to say, Well, existing security laws don’t apply. And, look, sometimes you need to be thoughtful about how new products and services do fit in within the existing legal regime.
But what’s troubling to me is when we see a suggestion that there is some type of blanket immunity or blanket exemption from existing legal requirements because something is so new. I think, you know, we need to have a presumption, a strong presumption, of all existing laws being adequate and applying, and the burden on the newcomers to actually prove why it might be that they may need certain tweaks, as opposed to the defaults being the other way.
Warzel: One response when you posted, I believe it was over the weekend, but sort of talking about this idea, Let’s remember that we have laws on the books, and these companies aren’t exempt—but there’s a feeling, I think, that some people think that just even the discussion of new regulatory frameworks: Is it just a distraction from the moment? And, you know, I do feel like that’s the case, because when the government was trying to regulate the social-media companies, there was a desire for some new paradigms or for, you know, a regulation that fit actually the new thing that these companies were doing. So don’t we need new frameworks for AI as well?
Khan: We absolutely may ultimately decide that we do need something concrete, but I think it’s important to be very precise about, where is it that our existing laws or existing regulatory regimes are falling short? You know, in this case, it seems like there is some activity that happens during the training itself, before these products hit the market, where you see employees saying, you know, This is where we actually need more oversight. You know, it’s been struggling to see that some of those recommendations seem to be more in the vein of, you know, self-regulation or voluntary compliance. Or maybe we have these third-party auditors, but there’s a very cozy relationship. And these specific technologies may be new, but there’s a long history of economic regulation spanning all the way back to the railroads, to telecom. And of course, these are all different tools and technologies. But there are important lessons for what does and doesn’t work.
Even in the blog post that spurred some of these recent conversations, the CEO referenced bank supervision as a potential analog, when you basically have people from the government that are more closely embedded within banks to try to assess certain types of risks. And so I think there is a long history of tools that we should be mining to figure out what makes sense here.
But I do think there’s this basic level in which something about the current conversation has seemed really off, where on the one hand, you have these companies declaring that the technologies and tools that they’re developing may end up having, you know, catastrophic effects alongside getting ready to go public and become billionaires and trillionaires overnight. I mean, if you just take those set of facts and apply it to every other industry, we would think that was ludicrous. And so I think that’s why we need to, you know, look at this AI exceptionalism that seems to be infecting the current conversation with some clear eyes.
Warzel: Yeah. I believe, like, three days after Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, said that there’s a reasonable chance that in six to 12 months, a bot swarm could take over the entire internet. He was at Salesforce, selling B2B software as a service to people, which is kind of an odd thing if you think extinction is coming.
In the in the case of the OpenAI incident where some of its models hacked the website Hugging Face, I wanted to get your perspective on: These are models, that they did behave differently than the trainers wanted them to do, but like, they hacked a website in that specific case. Do you think that OpenAI should face legal ramifications, like, for that instance?
Khan: It’s a very interesting question. And there are a whole set of laws that could potentially apply. But specifically when you’re thinking about the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, which is a criminal statute; criminal penalties apply. People have gone to jail for violating that statute. You know, there usually is an element of intent that you need to find. And so I you know, one thing that people have raised is, Okay, but what does it look like for models to have intent? And can you really ascribe that to the company? I think this also goes back to this basic question of what could have been reasonably known. And I think the more and more we’re getting additional information, it seems that this was not just an outlier incident.
There have actually been a whole set of events where models ended up acting in ways that, you know, the individuals did not want or foresee and may have committed a crime. And so I absolutely think that there is a point at which if you are aware that your technology and the models you’re working on have this capability, because you’re seeing it, and you’re continuing to allow those to act in this way, I think there is a very real question around intent and when that should actually attach.
Warzel: Yeah. Is it intent if you are creating these models to be as collaborative and as crafty and as intelligent and as good of problem solvers as possible?
Khan: I think the other issue here is, you know, a lot of the information that is available here is from this, you know, group called METR that’s comprised of—
Warzel: One of the monitoring groups.
Khan: The monitoring groups. And, you know, they are almost like a civic voluntary group that’s doing this work without any regulatory authority. And so it’s conditional on what information is being made available to them. Oftentimes, their reports are scoped to just look at the models. But I think there is a broader landscape that we need to understand about, What did humans know or should have known, and what, really, the company and should have been in a better position to prohibit or limit? And I think some of that is still pretty murky, because this report was scoped to focus so specifically on, you know, just the models and the agents themselves. So I do think we actually need a much bigger picture outside of the context of some, you know, voluntary inspection and more with the teeth of, you know, law enforcement and real regulation.
[Music]
Warzel: So you posted on X, you know, talking about this, weighing in, as we said: David Sacks whose investors, former Trump AI czar, publicly expressed agreement with your position, which then I saw a bunch of people, you know, doing the eyes emoji at that. And on one hand, it seems honestly a bit rich that someone like Sacks, who’s, you know, been a proponent of letting it rip with AI development, and also at one time part of a government that has deprioritized a lot of oversight and dismantled a lot of it. But is this also potentially a sign that AI is scrambling some of the traditional political coalitions?
Khan: It’s possible. I mean, that’s not particularly new to this moment. Even when you go back to the broader conversation around how to deal with the concentration of power that we were seeing in firms like Google and Amazon and Facebook, that was already starting to scramble some of that.
I mean, you know, back in 2019, I was working as a staffer for the House Judiciary Committee’s antitrust subcommittee, and we were doing an investigation into Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Apple. And, you know, we had instances where you had the most progressive member of that committee, you know, ask a question that sounded very similar to a question that the most conservative member on that committee was asking, because they were, you know, deeply concerned about concentrations of power. And so you had the House Progressive Caucus and the House Freedom Caucus, you know, actually working closely on some of this.
I think we saw some of that bipartisanship fissure during the last administration. But I think we saw it just, you know, totally in free fall this time around because, as you noted, one of the first things that the Trump administration did was not just halt existing investigations. They actually went and undid settlements that were already in place with some of these very companies. And so we’ve just seen, you know, a real free-for-all in terms of law enforcement, extremely deregulatory posture. DOGE, the effort has basically, you know, contributed to the dismantling of the administrative state.
And so, you know, while I will always be encouraged when there is kind of a broader set of people that want to align behind a position that I think is the right one, I think there has been something quite puzzling about people who were all for, you know, tearing down government to now be saying, Actually, the existing laws exist. And, you know, we need government to just enforce those.
Warzel: I’ve seen some of the debate around this AI moment framed as extinction versus regulatory capture. And I’m curious: On the regulatory-capture front, like, how do we avoid this becoming a moment where these companies are setting the conversation, right? Like, even the language that we’re seeing right now, they come out and they’re using this phrase pacing the frontier of AI development. And now everyone’s talking about pacing the frontier. Like, they are very good, it seems, at setting, you know, the terms that we all engage on. I’m curious, though: Like, how do we avoid the regulatory-capture stuff?
Khan: Yeah. I mean, there’s a long history here of how regulators do and don’t get captured. And some of that depends on how you set up the regulation. And is it designed to have, you know, a lot of coziness between the regulated party and the government? What kinds of safeguards do you put in place?
I think, you know, it would be shortsighted to have this conversation without talking about the role of money and politics and how just, you know, the overwhelming surge of money going into our elections also ends up having an effect where, you know, people who may be more in favor of regulating AI or regulating crypto have to keep in the back of their heads that if they go out on this, they’re going to see a, you know, huge funnel of cash come out against them.
And so I think that has been a core dynamic here too. I think as we, you know, think about What should we do here? Congress absolutely needs to be figuring out: How can it develop more of the technical expertise so that it can figure out what’s the right regime here? And I think we’ve been seeing, you know, for several decades now, a concerted project to limit the ability of Congress to do that. I mean, this goes all the way back to the 1994 Gingrich revolution, where there was an active effort to slash committee staff. There used to be an Office of Technology Assessment, where Congress used to have its own technical expertise in-house, and a lot of that was dismantled.
So I do think that this current conversation around What do we do about AI? is coming at a moment where we’ve seen this, you know, slow drumbeat of just total degradation of governing capability and governing capacity. And so the challenge is heightened for that very reason.
Warzel: If you were back at the FTC right now, if you were there at the helm, what concrete steps would you be taking as you’re watching politicians being really activated by this? As you’re watching public sentiment change, and people are, I think, rightfully very concerned when there’s extinction headlines, you know, at the top of The New York Times and The Atlantic and, you know, everywhere else?
Khan: Yeah. I mean, a few things. I do think that some of what’s been reported and what’s already publicly out there would very much warrant investigations and subpoenas being sent out to collect more information, some of which would be looking at: Have there been unfair practices—and unfair is, you know, a legal term of art here—where companies basically exposed people, expose companies to unreasonable levels of risk that resulted in real harm being done?
And I think one other interesting element here is: This industry is extremely interconnected, right. One of the first things that happened after the Hugging Face incident became public was it was announced: Nvidia was actually going to be buying up Hugging Face for billions of dollars. And that sets up an interesting question, because it was Hugging Face that was the harmed party from the OpenAI incident and would likely have, you know, standing to sue if they wanted to do that. But once they’re in-house at Nvidia, Nvidia’s incentives are not to be holding OpenAI accountable. And instead, we’ve been seeing their CEO, you know, cast some doubt about what they described as alarmism here.
And so I think the deeply interconnected nature of this industry, where you have an enormous amount of partnerships across investments, interdependencies, where the success of one company is really propping up your balance sheet, I think also is something to be understanding and inspecting.
And one of the investigations we were doing was into these partnerships to try to understand: How are these contracts written? What are companies actually saying that they’re going to be getting in return for their investments? If you see a big investment from, you know, a hyperscaler into one of these model companies, is that also coming with certain rights to shape the business strategy that could, you know, also result in implications to competition? So I think there’s a lot to unpack there.
I think there’s also just a lot to look at in terms of the bread-and-butter effects on people in their everyday lives. And so, you know, we’ve already seen some lawsuits filed privately against chatbots for, you know, engaging in conduct that families have said resulted in their kids taking their own lives. There are various cases that are still under way here. Many of those cases are brought under a product-liability framework—so alleging that, basically, you know, these were defective chatbots; these were defective products that resulted in grave harm to people in their families.
There’s also a question of basic tort law and the questions of negligence. And was there a reckless disregard in terms of certain safeguards that these companies should have put in place that weren’t? So I think there’s a lot to be exploring from a law-enforcement perspective. Some of those cases are being brought privately. But so far, you know, we saw the president tweet, We don’t need any new regulations. We have existing law enforcement, but—
Warzel: Hoax buster.
Khan: The Hoax buster. And instead we’re seeing, you know, an all-time low, effectively, in terms of criminal prosecutions and investigations.
Warzel: So this AI-safety conversation—part of the framing it as, you know, “existential rise of the machines,” “human race will be eliminated” type of thing—I think I fear that it is obscuring a lot of those personal harms to people, like what is happening to workers, like what is happening with the consolidation of the industry, as you said, with companies like Nvidia. Like, do you think that the extinction framework is unhelpful because it does obscure all of that? Like, we’re letting a lot of these real—we’re debating how powerful these things are when there’s powerful things that are happening right now as a result of, you know, these algorithms, of these products. Like, do you think this is all kind of a smoke screen, and we should be paying more attention to what’s happening right now with the harms?
Khan: I absolutely think we should be paying more attention to existing harms that are already happening. And, you know, there’s a broader conversation around affordability. And we all know that Americans are really feeling the heat when it comes to a cost-of-living crisis and, you know, under enormous strain in terms of paying rent, buying groceries; health-care costs are skyrocketing. And that sometimes is happening in a totally different space than this conversation.
But there are actually key ways and key places where what we’re seeing with AI could actually be contributing to the cost-of-living crisis. You know, we’ve already seen some firms be engaging in surveillance pricing when they’re using some of these AI tools, to basically serve up prices that are specifically targeted to what they know your pain point is. We’re seeing similar, you know, wage-management algorithms on the worker side. That could also be, basically depressing what workers are making. And so, you know, I think there are a whole set of ways in which these tools are already harming people in a day-to-day sense. And we absolutely need more attention on that.
You know, I think that when it comes to this question of extinction and what is really the harm here, I apply more of a risk-assessment framework. There is a huge information asymmetry between what people working in these companies know and what we, as outsiders or regulators or enforcers, know. And so I think we need to assess that risk, get more information. And if there are things that need to be done to put in place to prevent more of these models being so defective, I think we absolutely need to see that.
Warzel: Some of these AI CEOs have offered some specific ideas, Dario being the one with the—he likes to write really long blog posts. Maybe they’re not specific enough, but they are more specific, it seems, than, like, Mark Zuckerberg and, like, the Web 2 social-media giants who kind of just said, Regulate us, right. There’s the embedded company monitors that are independent, the idea of a slowdown. Like, do you think the things that are being proposed on their face are good ideas?
Khan: I think elements of it should be considered. I mean, I think this question of, you know, We have bank supervision as this long-standing thing should be on the table. Again, I think a lot of the devil’s going to be in the details in terms of: How are you structuring this, how much of this is just voluntary versus you’re actually on the hook for providing information, providing complete information? What are the ramifications if you actually violate some of these procedures?
So I think there are ways to structure this in a way that is relatively meaningless and toothless and just basically a fabrication of any accountability, versus structuring it so that you actually have real teeth and accountability. And so I think where you fall on that spectrum is going to be key. I do think, though, this goes back to who’s driving the conversation and who’s in the driver’s seat. And that’s where I do see a real asymmetry, where so much of the public response and the response from government is in a responsive posture and a reactive posture. And I think that can also have real downsides.
Warzel: The one thing that I think is different about these, or maybe it seems different, rather, the positioning of these AI CEOs, is some of them have, for a really long time, just been obsessively worrying about these issues. It’s not that they’ve devoted their careers to agonizing over, you know, the extinction of humanity, et cetera. I’m just curious, given that there’s always been this kind of safety realm, do you trust that these guys are being earnest about their fears?
Khan: I mean, I don’t see it as my job or really knowable as to, like, What are their internal motives? It certainly seems like, you know, some of the employees that are coming out of these firms, certainly seem to be earnest. I mean, I think there is this question of: At what point does somebody’s financial position line up with what they’re actually saying or not saying? And I think that’s where there’s a real question as to, if you are really committed to the belief that what your company is doing could lead to all of these harms, shouldn’t we be seeing much more extreme actions internally to stop it?
You know, I think one of the responses to the blog post has been: There’s absolutely nothing stopping you from slowing down the pace of these model development, and you don’t actually need an antitrust exemption. Right. And I think it was that call for an antitrust exemption that set off a lot of red flags for people, because it suggested that maybe what is being asked for is some type of regulatory immunity and diverting attention from the fact that these companies do have all the authority and ability to do what they say needs to be done.
[Music]
Warzel: One of the things that you do so well in your writing and in talking about this is drawing historical parallels. And I think in this moment, it feels very odd right now to have all these people talking about, you know, existential stuff. The pace of the news cycle is crazy with all of this. Can you offer some historical parallels for us all to just, like, latch on to here to feel like this is more of a normal type of industrial crisis, than something that is, you know, abnormal, and it’s just maybe playing out at abnormal speed?
Khan: Yeah. I mean, I want to reserve the idea that maybe there is something different here. And it’s not that analogies will get us all the way, but I think it’s absolutely true that if you go back and look at, you know, the advent of railroads, you know, there were some major railroad disasters that killed a lot of people when railroads started being, you know, interconnected across the country. Similar with, you know, cars. And there were all sorts of car-safety regulations that needed to be put in place.
The idea that you have a new technology that, admittedly, could do a lot of good but also, if not carefully managed and with a lot of safeguards, could do a lot of bad—we’ve encountered that in the past. And we’ve put obligations and requirements on the companies themselves to make sure they are not just letting loose into the wild new technologies that could have disastrous consequences.
And so I think that’s the part of the conversation that we need to go back to in terms of moving away from this AI exceptionalism and thinking in a clear-eyed way about: How is it that we’ve encountered prior technologies? How have we mitigated their risks? What are the government-oversight mechanisms that we’ve had in place to make sure that we’re not just seeing companies, you know, let out loose all of these products, and then the public is forced to do the cleanup on the back end after the executives and individuals have gotten phenomenally rich? And oh, by that time, they’re also going to be pouring all their wealth into actually blocking those regulations. Right? I think that is a cycle that we have seen, including with Web 2.0, that we very much need to be guarding against.
Warzel: So we have more control than we think we do, or than the labs are saying we do.
Khan: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it partly exists with existing government agencies, even in their more emaciated forms. There’s more that Congress could be doing, even from an oversight perspective and information-gathering. If partly what is leading to, you know, this asymmetric conversation is the huge information disadvantage that the public and government are at, I think there’s opportunity for Congress to be demanding that information.
Warzel: I think that’s a great place to leave it. Lina Khan, thank you so much.
Khan: Thanks so much.
[Music]
Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts these days. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener.
Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet.

articles.title: Mưa ngập đường, người dân TPHCM bì bõm về nhà
articles.text:
TPO - Tại khu vực phía Đông TPHCM, cơn mưa với lưu lượng lớn nhanh chóng gây ngập một số tuyến đường như Hoàng Hữu Nam, Lê Văn Việt... khiến người dân khổ sở để về nhà.
Tối 18/9, trên địa bàn TP. HCM xảy ra mưa to trên diện rộng. Cơn mưa to kèm theo dông, sét liên hồi. Ảnh: Ngô Tùng Trận mưa lớn trên địa bàn khu vực phía Đông TP. HCM. Video: Ngô TùngTại khu vực phía Đông thành phố, cơn mưa với lưu lượng lớn nhanh chóng gây ngập một số tuyến đường như Hoàng Hữu Nam (phường Long Bình), Lê Văn Việt (phường Tăng Nhơn Phú)... Ghi nhận tại đường Hoàng Hữu Nam, nhiều đoạn ngập sâu khiến các phương tiện lưu thông khó khăn và phải di chuyển chậm.
Cơn mưa lớn nhanh chóng khiến cả tuyến đường nhanh chóng thành "biển nước" mênh mông.Trên đường Lê Văn Việt, mưa to tạo sóng nước tại những đoạn trũng thấp.Đoạn đường gần cổng Đình Phong Phú ngập sâu gần lút bánh xe máy khiến việc đi lại hết sức khó khăn, nhiều người chọn cách tấp xe vào lề chờ bớt mưa và giảm ngập để có thể tiếp tục hành trình.Trận mưa lớn làm đường về nhà của mỗi người thêm chật vật, khó khăn.
Trong ngày 18/9, trên địa bàn TPHCM diễn ra nhiều trận mưa ở nhiều thời điểm khác nhau, với lưu lượng lớn. Theo Đài Khí tượng thủy văn Nam Bộ, từ 19h ngày 18/9 đến 19h ngày 20/9, khu vực TPHCM có mưa vừa, mưa to, có nơi mưa rất to. Tổng lượng mưa trong 48 giờ phổ biến 70-150 mm, có nơi trên 150 mm. Ảnh: Ngô Tùng.

articles.title: Du lịch Gia Lai ghi dấu tại Lễ hội Việt Nam ở Kanagawa, Nhật Bản
articles.text:
Gia Lai mở rộng kết nối, quảng bá điểm đến
Nằm trong chuỗi các hoạt động xúc tiến du lịch trọng điểm quốc gia năm 2026, chương trình quảng bá du lịch Gia Lai tại Lễ hội Việt Nam lần thứ 10 (Vietnam Festa in Kanagawa 2026); Bộ Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch phối hợp với chính quyền tỉnh Kanagawa đã tổ chức Hội thảo xúc tiến du lịch Việt Nam tại tỉnh Kanagawa, Nhật Bản. Hoạt động xúc tiến lần này được kỳ vọng mở thêm cơ hội kết nối doanh nghiệp, đường bay và thu hút khách Nhật đến Gia Lai.
Tại Hội thảo, Sở Văn hoá, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Gia Lai đã giới thiệu về du lịch tỉnh Gia Lai cung cấp thông tin, hình ảnh về các điểm đến, sản phẩm du lịch và giá trị di sản văn hóa Gia Lai đến người dân, du khách và cộng đồng người Việt Nam tại Kanagawa. Đây là bước đệm chiến lược đưa thương hiệu du lịch Gia Lai mới tỏa sáng tại thị trường Đông Bắc Á.
Sự xuất hiện của Gia Lai tại Hội thảo xúc tiến, quảng bá du lịch Việt Nam ở Kanagawa đã nhận được đánh giá rất cao từ chính quyền địa phương, Đại sứ quán Việt Nam và giới doanh nghiệp lữ hành Nhật Bản.
Phó giám đốc Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Gia Lai Nguyễn Thị Kim Chung nhấn mạnh thông điệp chuyển dịch mạnh mẽ từ giới thiệu tiềm năng sang chủ động cung cấp giải pháp sản phẩm cho từng phân khúc khách hàng Nhật Bản
Theo đó, Gia Lai định hình 5 dòng sản phẩm dành cho thị trường này, gồm nghỉ dưỡng biển chất lượng cao; du lịch văn hóa - di sản cộng đồng; khám phá thiên nhiên xanh; du lịch nông nghiệp và trải nghiệm văn hóa cà phê; du lịch golf kết hợp nghỉ dưỡng.
Cũng tại hội thảo, Gia Lai giới thiệu Nghị quyết hỗ trợ thu hút khách quốc tế qua các chuyến bay charter đến Cảng hàng không Phù Cát giai đoạn 2026-2027. Đây được xem là một trong những giải pháp tạo thêm động lực kết nối trực tiếp, góp phần mở rộng khả năng đưa khách quốc tế, trong đó có khách Nhật Bản, đến khu vực.
Cùng với đó, mạng lưới đường bay Việt Nam - Nhật Bản của Vietnam Airlines cũng được giới thiệu tại chương trình, tạo thêm thông tin cho các doanh nghiệp lữ hành hai nước trong việc xây dựng tour, kết nối điểm đến.
Tại không gian quảng bá, Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch Gia Lai cung cấp thông tin, hình ảnh về các điểm đến, sản phẩm du lịch và giá trị di sản văn hóa của tỉnh đến người dân, du khách và cộng đồng người Việt Nam tại Kanagawa.
Hoạt động giao lưu, kết nối doanh nghiệp được triển khai bằng hình thức quay số trúng thưởng. Với sự hỗ trợ của các doanh nghiệp lữ hành trong tỉnh, Gia Lai trao tặng 43 voucher cho đại biểu đến từ các đơn vị lữ hành quốc tế Nhật Bản, qua đó tạo thêm cơ hội để doanh nghiệp hai bên tìm hiểu, kết nối sản phẩm.
Từ "gian hàng" đến những kết nối du lịch cụ thể
Trước đó, Phó giám đốc Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Gia Lai Nguyễn Thị Kim Chung đã có buổi trao đổi với Thống đốc tỉnh Kanagawa Kuroiwa Yuji. Thống đốc Kanagawa bày tỏ sự chào đón đối với Gia Lai khi tham gia Lễ hội Việt Nam lần thứ 10 - sự kiện được người dân Nhật Bản và tỉnh Kanagawa luôn hào hứng chào đón mỗi năm.
Thống đốc Kuroiwa Yuji cũng bày tỏ sự ấn tượng với gian trưng bày quảng bá du lịch của tỉnh Gia Lai. Qua gian trưng bày ông đã hiểu hơn về Gia Lai và ấn tượng với "Nón ngựa Phú Gia".
Thống đốc Kanagawa mong muốn tiếp tục mong muốn tiếp tục kết nối xúc tiến, quảng bá du lịch với Gia Lai và các địa phương ở Việt Nam để nhiều người dân Nhật Bản đến Việt Nam tham quan và trải nghiệm nét đẹp văn hóa trong thời gian tới.
Trong 2 ngày diễn ra Lễ hội Việt Nam lần thứ 10 tại Kanagawa, gian hàng Gia Lai thu hút sự quan tâm của nhiều doanh nghiệp du lịch, lữ hành và hàng nghìn người dân Nhật Bản. Du khách tìm hiểu về các điểm đến biển, cao nguyên, văn hóa, làng nghề truyền thống; đồng thời trực tiếp trải nghiệm cà phê và các sản phẩm OCOP của Gia Lai.
Chị Ayn - một người dân tại Nhật Bản tham quan gian hàng của tỉnh Gia Lai và cho biết: "Tôi đã học tiếng Việt tại thành phố Hồ Chí Minh. Tôi đã đi nhiều nơi ở Việt Nam.
Một du khách khác người Nhật khác đặc biệt thích thú với chiếc "Nón ngựa Phú Gia" và những họa tiết trang trí trong chiếc nón.
"Tôi sẽ đến Gia Lai để tìm hiểu về làng nghề truyền thống này", du khách thích thú chia sẻ sau khi đội thử nón và chụp hình tại gian hàng.
Lễ hội Việt Nam lần thứ 10 tại Kanagawa năm 2026 đánh dấu cột mốc quan trọng trong mối quan hệ hợp tác giao lưu văn hóa giữa hai nước. Sự hiện diện chủ động của Gia Lai bên cạnh các hoạt động chính trị, ngoại giao giao lưu văn hóa đã khẳng định vị thế và hình ảnh của một địa phương sẵn sàng hội nhập.
Với việc giới thiệu các sản phẩm chuyên biệt cho thị trường Nhật Bản, kết nối doanh nghiệp và mở rộng thông tin về khả năng tiếp cận bằng đường hàng không, Gia Lai đang từng bước đưa hình ảnh "Đại ngàn chạm Biển xanh" đến gần hơn với thị trường khách quốc tế trong Năm Du lịch Quốc gia 2026.
